newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan's new trade policy seen ambitious.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan's new trade policy seen ambitious.

text.p: Pakistan is unlikely to reduce a yawning trade gap as sought by its new trade policy for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June), analysts said on Thursday.
Commerce Minister Ishaq Dar on Wednesday unveiled the trade policy aiming at bringing the trade deficit down to $2.33 billion, or 30.86 percent less, from $3.37 billion in 1996/97.

Dar, announcing the policy for 1997/98 after approval by Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's cabinet, said exports were to grow 15 percent to $9.575 billion from the last year's $8.26 billion and imports to $11.9 billion from 11.63 billion.
Analysts said the export growth target was too ambitious as most of the incentives given to boost exports would take more than a year or two before giving results.
"The targets are not realistic," analyst Zuna Mansoor of ING Baring Securities told Reuters.

"We believe the government is making a sincere effort to improve the country's trade balance, particularly as the trade policy focuses largely on actual implementation systems rather than wishful thinking.
"However, we believe that it will be difficult to meet the trade deficit target of $2.3 billion, and we expect this to be close to $2.9 billion," she said.

Aziz Anis Dhedhy of Indosuez W.I. Carr Securities said the target seemed to be slightly optimistic as most of the policy measures are long-term in nature and might not result in immediate export growth.

"Export inflation of 16.7 percent as envisaged in the trade policy is not possible, at least not in the immediate future," Dhedy said, adding: "Even a 10 percent rise should be seen an achievement and success of the policy."
"The conceptual framework of the policy is right and the direction is very important, which should improve the sentiment, but fundamentals do not change overnight," he said.
Analysts said Pakistan had an inflexible import base largely based on essential food, petroleum, chemicals and machinery items, which may keep the import bill high.
They said more than 60 percent of exports were cotton-based and prone to weather vagaries and other factors bearing on the cotton crop.

"Exporters should be happier as the policy is more substantial on removing big and small hurdles in the export process, but there is nothing extraordinary that suggests a drastic rise in exports," Mansoor said.
Dar said 50 percent of the duty drawback to exporters would now be paid within three days of presentation of documents and the balance after verification of customs authorities.

Dhedy said allowing duty drawback on all inputs, including fuel for export of cement, might not result in large export orders as domestic cement prices would remain uncompetitive despite the duty drawbacks because of cement oversupply.
